factors.factor: Single primary database with a single secondary, making the primary a single point of failure and forcing all load onto one database
factors.evidence: "GitLab.com currently uses a single primary and a single secondary in hot-standby mode... In this setup a single database has to handle all the load, which is not ideal."

factors.factor: Sudden database load spike (suspected spam plus an accidentally scheduled background data-removal job triggered by an abuse flag) caused replication lag and WAL segments to be removed before the secondary could consume them
factors.evidence: "GitLab.com starts experiencing an increase in database load due to what we suspect was spam... part of the load was caused by a background job trying to remove a GitLab employee and their associated data." and "The replication failed as WAL segments needed by the secondary were already removed from the primary."

factors.factor: No WAL archiving, so the secondary could not catch up and had to be manually re-synchronised
factors.evidence: "As GitLab.com was not using WAL archiving, the secondary had to be re-synchronised manually."

factors.factor: Undocumented pg_basebackup behaviour (it waits silently for the primary to start replication) and a lack of shared operational knowledge in runbooks led to prolonged troubleshooting and misdiagnosis
factors.evidence: "pg_basebackup will wait for the primary to start sending over replication data and it will sit and wait silently until that time. Unfortunately this was not clearly documented in our engineering runbooks nor in the official pg_basebackup document."

factors.factor: An overly high max_connections setting (8000), applied almost a year earlier and never reviewed, prevented PostgreSQL from restarting when max_wal_senders was raised and delayed re-synchronisation
factors.evidence: "In our case this was set to 8000. Such a value is way too high, yet it had been applied almost a year ago and was working fine until that point."

factors.factor: No safeguards distinguished the primary from the secondary when running destructive commands, so a data directory wipe intended for the secondary was executed on the primary
factors.evidence: "an engineer proceeds to wipe the PostgreSQL database directory, errantly thinking they were doing so on the secondary. Unfortunately this process was executed on the primary instead."

factors.factor: Backup procedure silently broken: pg_dump 9.2 used against PostgreSQL 9.6, so no usable backups existed
factors.evidence: "the backup procedure was using pg_dump 9.2, while our database is running PostgreSQL 9.6... A difference in major versions results in pg_dump producing an error, terminating the backup procedure." | "Hoping they could restore the database the engineers involved went to look for the database backups, and asked for help on Slack. Unfortunately the process of both finding and using backups failed completely."

factors.factor: Backup failures went undetected because cron failure notification emails were rejected by the receiving mail system (DMARC not configured for them), and there was no independent alert on missing backups
factors.evidence: "Unfortunately DMARC was not enabled for the cronjob emails, resulting in them being rejected by the receiver. This means we were never aware of the backups failing, until it was too late."

factors.factor: Azure disk snapshots not enabled for database servers, and cross-account snapshot restore is very slow, limiting recovery options
factors.evidence: "these snapshots were not enabled for any of the database servers as we assumed that our other backup procedures were sufficient enough." and "in one such case it took over a week to restore a snapshot."

factors.factor: Slow, low-performance staging storage (no premium storage) made data copying the main recovery bottleneck
factors.evidence: "For our staging environment we were using Azure classic, without Premium Storage... the disks are very slow, resulting in them being the main bottleneck in the restoration process." and "Copying the data from the staging to the production host took around 18 hours."

factors.factor: Recovery point limited to a stale LVM snapshot, not designed for disaster recovery, increasing data loss
factors.evidence: "The LVM snapshots are primarily used to easily copy data from our production environment to our staging environment... the produced snapshots are not really meant to be used for disaster recovery."

action_items.action: Enable WAL archiving (continuous archiving to object storage) on the production PostgreSQL primary so replicas can catch up after lag without a full manual re-synchronisation.
Fix the pg_dump backup job to use the PostgreSQL client binaries matching the production server version, and add an automated check that fails if the backup is missing, empty, or older than 24 hours.
Configure cron job failure notifications to comply with DMARC and add a dead-man's-switch alert that fires when an expected successful backup has not been recorded.

Add safeguards to destructive data directory operations, such as host-identity checks, confirmation prompts, and read-only mounts or role-based restrictions, so that wiping a data directory on the primary is not possible by accident.
Schedule and document regular restore drills from pg_dump and other backup sources, including timed measurements of restore duration, to verify that recovery procedures work before they are needed.
Enable Azure disk snapshots for all database servers and evaluate faster cross-account or same-account restore options to reduce restore times that currently can take over a week.
Document pg_basebackup's silent wait-for-primary behaviour in the engineering runbooks and add a timeout and progress indicator to the replica rebuild procedure.
Audit PostgreSQL configuration parameters across all servers, correcting unreasonable values such as max_connections set to 8000, and add config validation to catch such settings.
Move staging database storage to premium/SSD-backed disks or an equivalent faster option so that restores and data copies are not bottlenecked by slow disks.
Establish a separate, dedicated disaster-recovery backup path rather than relying on staging LVM snapshots, and set a defined recovery point objective for production data.
Add a database read/write load-balancing and capacity plan, reducing dependence on a single primary, and review background jobs (such as user data removal) to rate-limit or batch heavy deletions.
